title: Phase I Metabolism & Cytochrome P450s
summary: The oxidation machinery of the liver and how it attacks drugs.

lessons.title: The CYP450 catalytic cycle

levels.kid:
Your liver has tiny machines that change drug molecules. One big family is called **CYP450**. Picture a machine with an iron tool at its center. It grabs a drug and uses oxygen to add a new piece, often making the drug easier to wash away.

The machine needs power. A helper passes it electrons, a little like charging a battery. It grabs oxygen from the air you breathed. After several steps, one oxygen atom joins the drug and the other becomes water.

But the machine can also make a drug work for the first time, or create a harmful new piece. That is why chemists test what comes out of the machine, not just how quickly the original drug disappears. Different people have different amounts and versions of these machines.
levels.hs:
**Cytochrome P450 (CYP)** enzymes are iron-containing proteins that oxidize many drugs. Most drug-metabolizing CYPs sit in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells (also in gut and other tissues). Their heme iron is held by a cysteine sulfur.

The usual reaction is **monooxygenation**: drug + O2 + reducing power from NADPH → drug with one added O atom + water. The second O atom becomes water. A helper enzyme, **NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase**, passes electrons from NADPH to the CYP heme.

The simplified cycle: (1) drug binds near iron; (2) iron gains an electron; (3) O2 binds; (4) a second electron arrives and protons help break the O-O bond; (5) a highly reactive iron-oxo species, **Compound I**, adds O to the drug; (6) the product leaves.

For a C-H bond, Compound I takes H to form a carbon radical, then an OH group rebounds onto that carbon. The result is a new C-OH bond.

The name P450 comes from the enzyme's characteristic light absorption at 450 nm when its reduced iron binds carbon monoxide. The cycle sometimes "uncouples," making reactive oxygen instead of a drug metabolite.
levels.college:
**Architecture.** Microsomal drug-metabolizing CYPs are heme-thiolate monooxygenases. Resting heme is ferric (Fe3+) with a distal water ligand. Substrate binding displaces water and often shifts Fe to high spin, raising its reduction potential. NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR, an FAD/FMN enzyme) supplies the first electron, giving ferrous Fe2+.

**Catalytic cycle.** Ferrous heme binds O2 (oxyferrous complex). A second electron arrives from CPR or sometimes cytochrome b5, generating a peroxo intermediate. Sequential protonation yields ferric hydroperoxo **Compound 0**; O-O heterolysis releases water and gives **Compound I**, an Fe(IV)=O porphyrin radical cation. Compound I abstracts H from an aliphatic C-H; the carbon radical rapidly recombines with Fe-OH (**oxygen rebound**) to give an alcohol, restoring ferric heme. Overall: RH + O2 + NADPH + H+ → ROH + H2O + NADP+.

**Alternative chemistry.** CYPs also epoxidize alkenes, N- or S-oxidize heteroatoms, and perform dealkylation through unstable hydroxylated intermediates. The substrate's orientation in the pocket determines which atom approaches Compound I.

**Uncoupling.** If oxygen activation is not productively coupled, superoxide, H2O2 or water can form without substrate oxidation, wasting NADPH.

**History.** Reduced CO-bound CYP has an absorbance maximum near 450 nm; that spectral signature named P450. The proximal cysteine thiolate helps stabilize the high-valent oxidant; replacing it disrupts catalysis.
levels.phd:
**Electronic mechanism.** Substrate entry displaces the sixth ligand (water) from low-spin ferric heme, often creating a five-coordinate high-spin state with higher reduction potential. CPR transfers electrons via FAD and FMN. The Fe(II)-O2 adduct is often described as Fe(III)-O2•− by resonance. The second electron yields a ferric peroxo species; delivery of two protons in a controlled network forms the hydroperoxo "Compound 0" and then cleaves O-O heterolytically. Cysteinate's electron-donating proximal "push" and distal acid/alcohol residues facilitate formation of Compound I (formal FeIV=O, porphyrin π-cation radical).

**Hydrogen abstraction/rebound.** A high-valent oxo abstracts H from substrate, generating FeIV-OH and a substrate radical. Radical rebound forms ROH, but radical rearrangements or cage escape may occur. Kinetic isotope effects from C-H vs C-D substitution can implicate H abstraction as rate-limiting, though measured isotope effects can be masked by commitment or preceding steps. The active site can switch selectivity by changing substrate orientation, not merely bond-dissociation energy.

**Shunts.** The peroxide shunt can deliver oxidizing equivalents from peroxides without the full two-electron NADPH/O2 pathway in experimental systems. Uncoupling branches may release superoxide after oxyferrous decay or H2O2 after hydroperoxo decay. Catalytic efficiency is product formed per NADPH consumed, distinct from turnover number.

**Inhibition.** Nitrogen-containing ligands (azole antifungals) can coordinate ferric heme and displace water (type II spectral shift), while substrates that displace water give a type I shift. Time-dependent mechanism-based inactivation can damage or tightly ligate heme after enzyme-dependent bioactivation. A spectral shift alone is not proof of clinical inhibition.

**Spatial biology.** Liver and gut CYPs reside mainly on the cytosolic face of ER membranes; their lipid microenvironment and CPR:cytochrome ratios can alter kinetics. Some steroidogenic CYPs instead reside in mitochondria and use a different electron-transfer chain.
levels.expert:
**How to investigate a clearance problem.** First identify the human enzyme using chemical inhibitors, recombinant CYPs and hepatocyte data; then determine the product's structure by LC-MS/MS. When a compound disappears in microsomes only with NADPH, CYP-mediated oxidation is plausible. When it disappears without NADPH, hydrolysis or another pathway is more likely. Confirm in hepatocytes because microsomes lack many cytosolic enzymes and transport.

**Mechanistic interpretation.** A high substrate-binding affinity does not ensure rapid turnover: orientation, electron delivery, formation of Compound I and product release all matter. A bulky substrate can bind strongly but poorly align its metabolic soft spot. Mixed or non-Michaelis kinetics are common with CYP3A4 due to multiple substrate binding and cooperative effects; avoid simple clearance predictions from one concentration.

**Drug interactions.** Competitive inhibitors occupy the catalytic site; azoles can also coordinate heme. Time-dependent inhibitors require preincubation with NADPH to reveal loss of activity; compare IC50 with and without preincubation and check reversibility after dilution. Induction is slower: nuclear receptors alter enzyme expression over days. Grapefruit furanocoumarins inactivate intestinal CYP3A4, so first-pass exposure can change without a proportionate effect on IV clearance.

**Assay traps.** Microsomal protein binding lowers unbound substrate concentration; correcting intrinsic clearance matters for lipophilic compounds. Depletion does not tell you whether the metabolite is active or toxic. Poor CYP coupling may yield ROS in vitro without clinical harm, while low-abundance reactive metabolites can matter despite small total clearance.

**Practical decision.** A medicinal chemist asks whether to block oxidation, alter binding orientation, reduce lipophilicity, or accept the pathway; fixing clearance by adding F can create a more potent inhibitor of another CYP. The goal is predictable human exposure and safety, not maximal metabolic stability.

keyPoints: CYPs are heme-thiolate monooxygenases, mainly in liver and gut ER
CPR supplies electrons from NADPH; O2 supplies an O atom to the substrate
Compound I is Fe(IV)=O with a porphyrin radical cation
C-H hydroxylation proceeds by H abstraction then oxygen rebound
Uncoupling can form superoxide or H2O2 without productive metabolism
P450 refers to reduced CO-bound heme absorption near 450 nm

lessons.title: Oxidations: hydroxylation, dealkylation, epoxidation

levels.kid:
The CYP machine can add oxygen to different places on a drug. If it adds an OH piece to a carbon, that is called **hydroxylation**. The new OH can help the drug mix with water.

Sometimes it snips off a little side group attached to oxygen or nitrogen. That is **dealkylation**. The side group does not vanish: it becomes a tiny separate molecule.

If a drug has a double bond, CYP can put an oxygen bridge across it. That bridge is an **epoxide**, a three-atom ring. Some epoxides are useful or harmless, but others react with important cell parts.

Changing a drug can make it easier to remove, switch it on, or make it unsafe. Scientists measure the new molecules rather than guessing from the original drug alone.
levels.hs:
CYPs perform several kinds of **oxidation**. They are often called Phase I reactions because they introduce or reveal a polar group for possible later conjugation. Phase I does not always happen before Phase II.

- **Hydroxylation:** adds an OH to a C-H site. Benzylic carbons (next to a benzene ring) are common targets. Aromatic hydroxylation may pass through an arene oxide before a phenol forms.
- **N-dealkylation:** removes an alkyl group from nitrogen, often converting a tertiary amine to a secondary amine. Diazepam can become nordiazepam this way.
- **O-dealkylation:** removes an alkyl group from oxygen, often revealing a phenol. CYP2D6 converts codeine to morphine by O-demethylation.
- **Epoxidation:** adds oxygen across a double bond, creating a three-membered ring. Carbamazepine forms an active 10,11-epoxide, later hydrolyzed by epoxide hydrolase.

An epoxide can be electrophilic, meaning it can react with proteins or DNA. But not every epoxide is dangerous; its stability, exposure and detoxification determine risk.

Remember: CYP oxidation can inactivate a drug, activate a prodrug, or produce a toxic metabolite. No single rule covers every molecule.
levels.college:
**Site selection.** C-H hydroxylation usually prefers accessible bonds with lower bond-dissociation energy (benzylic, allylic, tertiary), but CYP active-site orientation often overrides intrinsic reactivity. Aromatic hydroxylation can proceed by electrophilic addition to form an arene oxide or via direct insertion-like pathways; an NIH shift may move a ring substituent during rearrangement to phenol.

**Dealkylation mechanism.** N- and O-dealkylation begin with α-carbon hydroxylation adjacent to the heteroatom. The unstable carbinolamine (N) or hemiacetal (O) fragments to an amine or phenol plus a carbonyl coproduct (often formaldehyde from a methyl). Diazepam N-demethylation gives nordiazepam; codeine O-demethylation via CYP2D6 gives morphine. Genetic variation in CYP2D6 changes that conversion.

**Epoxidation.** Compound I adds across a C=C or aromatic π bond. Carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide retains anticonvulsant activity and is further converted to a diol by epoxide hydrolase. Aflatoxin B1's 8,9-epoxide is a potent DNA-reactive species; it is a toxin example, not a drug metabolite. Reactive metabolites may be trapped by glutathione.

**Other CYP routes.** N-oxidation produces amine N-oxides; S-oxidation produces sulfoxides/sulfones. Oxidative deamination can remove an amino group. Oxidative desulfuration replaces sulfur with oxygen in certain P=S compounds. CYP-mediated oxidation of acetaminophen produces a small amount of electrophilic NAPQI, usually trapped by glutathione.

**Purpose.** Map the whole metabolite profile: a fall in parent-drug concentration cannot distinguish safe clearance from active or reactive metabolites.
levels.phd:
**What determines regioselectivity?** Product ratios arise from a combination of substrate binding modes, access-channel kinetics, orientation relative to Compound I and competing transition-state barriers. The "weakest C-H gets oxidized" heuristic fails when that bond cannot approach the oxo. Deuterium labeling can reveal a kinetic isotope effect and metabolic switching, but isotopic substitution may shift binding poses too.

**Hydroxylation channels.** Aliphatic hydroxylation follows H abstraction/radical rebound in many CYPs. Aromatic oxidation may involve arene oxide formation and 1,2-migration (NIH shift), though isotope effects, quantum calculations and product distributions support multiple pathways depending on enzyme and substrate. Arene oxides can rearrange to phenols or be intercepted by epoxide hydrolase/GSH.

**Dealkylation bookkeeping.** α-H abstraction on an N-methyl group yields the α-hydroxylated intermediate; C-N scission gives formaldehyde and the demethylated amine. O-demethylation analogously gives formaldehyde and phenol. For larger alkyl groups, the carbonyl coproduct is an aldehyde or ketone depending on the α-carbon substitution. The dealkylated metabolite can be more active than the parent, as codeine→morphine demonstrates.

**Epoxide fates.** Carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide is pharmacologically active; microsomal epoxide hydrolase converts it to the corresponding trans-diol. Aflatoxin B1 exo-8,9-epoxide forms N7-guanine DNA adducts. Benzo[a]pyrene activation can involve sequential CYP and epoxide-hydrolase reactions, a reminder that hydrolysis does not always detoxify.

**NAPQI.** CYP2E1, CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 can oxidize acetaminophen to NAPQI; normally GSH captures it. This low-fraction route becomes hazardous when GSH is depleted.

**Drug-design test.** Metabolite ID, isotope tracing and GSH trapping should follow a new oxidation-site block: eliminating one route can increase flow into a worse one.
levels.expert:
**A real metabolite-ID workflow.** Incubate a compound in human hepatocytes and microsomes with appropriate cofactors, collect time points, and compare high-resolution MS features to parent. A +16 mass shift suggests oxygen addition, but could be hydroxylation, N-oxide, sulfoxide or epoxide; standards, MS/MS and sometimes NMR locate the site. A −14 shift can suggest demethylation, yet other transformations may share the mass difference. Do not label a metabolite from mass alone.

**Prioritize risk by exposure.** An epoxide drawn on a mechanism slide is not automatically dangerous. Ask how much forms, whether it survives to reach proteins/DNA, whether epoxide hydrolase and GSH handle it, and whether species differ. Reactive metabolite trapping with GSH and protein-adduct assays complement, but do not replace, safety studies.

**Activation matters.** Codeine's CYP2D6 O-demethylation generates morphine; strong CYP2D6 inhibition or poor-metabolizer genotype reduces conversion, while ultrarapid metabolism can increase it. Carbamazepine's epoxide is active and can contribute to adverse effects. If you block parent oxidation, exposure to active metabolites may fall while parent exposure rises.

**Avoid simplistic fixes.** Deuterating an oxidative soft spot can slow one pathway, but alternative sites may compensate. Fluorinating a benzylic carbon may change potency, permeability and toxicity. A metabolically stable analog is not automatically safer if clearance slows excessively.

**Communication.** Report parent and major metabolite exposure, enzyme assignment, reactive-metabolite signals and uncertainty separately. In a clinical program, changes in metabolite formation can cause interactions even when parent AUC moves little. A sharp in vitro finding is a hypothesis until human-relevant data support it.

keyPoints: Hydroxylation adds OH to carbon; accessible benzylic/allylic sites often react
N/O-dealkylation starts with α-carbon hydroxylation then bond cleavage
Codeine O-demethylation by CYP2D6 yields morphine
Epoxidation can yield active carbamazepine epoxide or reactive electrophiles
A +16 mass shift alone does not identify the oxidation type
CYP oxidation can activate, deactivate or bioactivate to toxicity

examples.tr: Reveals a phenolic OH and changes pharmacologic activity.
α-Carbon hydroxylation precedes C-N bond cleavage.
An active metabolite, later hydrolyzed to a diol.

lessons.title: Reductions & hydrolyses

levels.kid:
Not every drug change adds oxygen. Sometimes a body enzyme **reduces** a drug, giving it electrons or hydrogen. It is like putting something back into a simpler form. A colored drug piece might lose part of what made it colored.

Other enzymes use water to cut a bond. That is **hydrolysis**. Imagine water helping scissors cut a string. Ester links are often easy to cut. Amide links are often tougher.

Some medicines are designed to be cut on purpose. One medicine for blood pressure, enalapril, has a piece that gets removed so it can work well. The active product is called enalaprilat.

Your gut bacteria also change some drug molecules. Because many different helpers are involved, scientists test liver cells, blood and gut microbes to learn what really happens.
levels.hs:
Phase I metabolism includes not only oxidation but also **reduction** and **hydrolysis**. Reduction adds electrons or removes oxygen from a functional group. Hydrolysis breaks a bond by adding water. These reactions may activate or deactivate a drug.

**Reduction examples.** Nitro groups can be reduced to amines by intestinal microbes and some human enzymes. Gut bacteria reduce azo bonds (-N=N-) in sulfasalazine, releasing 5-aminosalicylic acid in the colon. Carbonyl reductases convert some ketones to alcohols, adding a new OH and sometimes creating a chiral center. NQO1 can reduce a quinone to a hydroquinone in a two-electron step.

**Hydrolysis examples.** Carboxylesterases (CES1, CES2) break ester bonds. Enalapril is an ester prodrug hydrolyzed to active enalaprilat. Irinotecan is activated to SN-38 by CES enzymes (CES2 is important in the intestine). Clopidogrel has a competing esterase route that inactivates much of the parent before CYP activation.

Epoxide hydrolase adds water across an epoxide ring, usually reducing its reactivity, though some pathways later produce harmful metabolites. Peptidases break peptide amides.

A drug's fate depends on which enzymes see it, not just on whether the molecule has a breakable bond.
levels.college:
**Reductions.** Nitro-to-amine proceeds through nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates; some intermediates are reactive, so "reduction" does not automatically mean detoxification. Azo reduction by gut bacteria cleaves sulfasalazine into 5-aminosalicylic acid (local anti-inflammatory) and sulfapyridine. Carbonyl reductases (CBR1/3, AKRs) reduce ketones to secondary alcohols using NADPH, sometimes altering stereochemistry and activity. NQO1 performs two-electron quinone reduction, often avoiding semiquinone radical redox cycling, though hydroquinones can reoxidize.

**Ester hydrolysis.** CES1 is abundant in liver, CES2 in intestine and liver. CES1 tends to accept substrates with a larger acyl group and small alcohol group; CES2 often favors smaller acyl and larger alcohol groups, but these are tendencies, not rules. CES1 hydrolyzes enalapril to enalaprilat; CES2 helps activate irinotecan to SN-38. Clopidogrel is mainly inactivated by carboxylesterase hydrolysis to an inactive carboxylic acid, competing with CYP-dependent formation of its active thiol metabolite. Plasma butyrylcholinesterase hydrolyzes certain ester-like drugs.

**Other hydrolases.** Microsomal epoxide hydrolase opens epoxide rings by water addition (carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide → trans-diol). Amidases and peptidases hydrolyze amides/peptides; rates vary widely. Aspirin undergoes ester hydrolysis to salicylate, including by esterases.

**Important exception.** Epoxide hydrolase's diol product can undergo another oxidation to a DNA-reactive diol epoxide (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene), so even hydrolysis can be part of a bioactivation sequence.
levels.phd:
**Redox networks beyond CYP.** The cellular NADPH/NADP+ and NADH/NAD+ pools drive reductases. Carbonyl reductases and aldo-keto reductases stereoselectively reduce ketones; whether the alcohol is more polar or more active depends on its structure and conjugation. Nitro group reduction can pass through nitroso and hydroxylamine states that form adducts or redox-cycle; bacterial oxygen-sensitive reductases make intestinal metabolism especially important for azo/nitro drugs. Quinone one-electron reduction (some CYP reductase pathways) generates semiquinone radicals and ROS; NQO1's obligate two-electron route can be protective but may also bioactivate specific quinones.

**Carboxylesterase catalysis.** CES enzymes use a serine-histidine-acid catalytic triad: serine attacks the ester, an acyl-enzyme forms, then water resolves it. CES1 and CES2 are ER-lumen enzymes with different substrate-preference pockets and expression. Enalapril hydrolysis (CES1) and irinotecan activation (CES2) illustrate why tissue distribution changes outcome. Rodents have plasma esterases with activities not directly predictive of humans.

**Epoxide hydrolase.** Microsomal EPHX1 uses an Asp nucleophile to open an epoxide, creating a covalent intermediate then a vicinal trans-diol. Carbamazepine epoxide is detoxified by this route, though its diol may retain effects. Benzo[a]pyrene's trans-diol can be re-epoxidized to a DNA-binding diol epoxide, demonstrating sequential activation despite a detoxifying-looking hydrolysis step.

**Gene/environment interactions.** Microbiome composition affects azo reduction. CES expression and CES1 variants can alter activation of ester prodrugs. Hypoxic tumor regions can favor nitro reduction, a design rationale for hypoxia-activated compounds; translating this to clinical selectivity is difficult.

**Experimental control.** Compare incubations with and without NADPH, specific esterase inhibitors, human plasma, hepatocytes and gut bacterial systems; buffer hydrolysis alone does not assign an enzyme.
levels.expert:
**When a compound disappears without NADPH, do not blame CYP.** Run a stability matrix: buffer, human plasma, heat-inactivated plasma, liver microsomes ± NADPH, hepatocytes and intestinal S9. Esterases are common, but chemical hydrolysis or microbial metabolism may dominate. Identify actual products before changing the scaffold.

**Prodrug case.** Enalapril's ester promotes oral absorption; hepatic CES1 generates active enalaprilat. A related design might fail if the target population has altered CES expression, or if competing hydrolysis occurs before absorption. In irinotecan, CES-mediated activation yields SN-38, then UGT1A1 inactivates it by glucuronidation; both steps influence exposure.

**Clinical contrast.** Clopidogrel's major hydrolysis route is inactivation; only a minority proceeds through CYP bioactivation. Increasing hydrolysis would decrease active thiol formation. The same enzyme family can activate one compound and deactivate another: classify by metabolite activity, never by reaction label.

**Microbiome caution.** Sulfasalazine's azo bond is designed to reach the colon for bacterial cleavage. Broad-spectrum antibiotics or altered microbiota can change this, but do not infer a specific clinical effect without data.

**Reactive metabolites.** A nitro group can become a hydroxylamine intermediate with toxicity potential. Epoxide hydrolysis often reduces electrophilicity but can supply a diol for later bioactivation. NQO1 may protect against radical cycling, yet substrate-specific quinone reductions may regenerate toxic intermediates.

**Design response.** If hydrolysis is unwanted, first test steric protection or replacement of the ester, then measure solubility and permeability. If it is required for activation, tune rate and tissue selectivity rather than abolish it. Species differences are large enough that human-derived matrices are essential for confidence.

Clopidogrel esterase hydrolysis is an inactivating competing pathway

lessons.title: Major isoforms: 3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 2C19, 1A2

levels.kid:
The CYP family has different workers. Each has a name like **3A4** or **2D6**. The names tell you they are related but not identical. Each worker likes different molecules.

If a person has a slower version of a worker, a drug may stay in their body longer. If that worker was supposed to switch the drug on, though, the drug may work less well instead.

Some foods or other medicines can slow a worker down. Other things can make the liver build more workers. For example, a part of grapefruit can slow 3A4 in the intestine.

Scientists study which worker handles a medicine and whether the person has a different version. This helps explain why the same medicine can affect people differently. Never assume a CYP name alone tells the whole story.
levels.hs:
Human CYPs have numbered families and subfamilies. The name **CYP2D6** means CYP family 2, subfamily D, gene 6. The major drug-handling isoforms include 3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 2C19 and 1A2.

- **3A4:** handles many drugs, has a large flexible active site, and is present in liver and intestine. Ketoconazole inhibits it; rifampin induces it. Grapefruit furanocoumarins inhibit intestinal 3A4.
- **2D6:** heavily affected by genetic variation. It converts codeine to morphine and helps activate tamoxifen to endoxifen. Some people are poor or ultrarapid metabolizers. Fluoxetine is a strong inhibitor.
- **2C9:** metabolizes S-warfarin and some NSAIDs. Genetic variants can slow clearance.
- **2C19:** helps activate clopidogrel; loss-of-function variants make activation weaker. It also metabolizes some proton-pump inhibitors.
- **1A2:** metabolizes caffeine and clozapine; tobacco smoke induces it, so stopping smoking can change exposure.

**Inhibition** starts relatively quickly when an inhibitor blocks an enzyme. **Induction** requires making more enzyme, so it develops and fades more slowly. A patient taking several medicines may experience both genetic and interaction effects.
levels.college:
**CYP3A4/5.** The 3A family has a broad, flexible active site and handles a large fraction of marketed drugs; 3A4 is abundant in liver and small-intestinal enterocytes. Midazolam is a common probe substrate. Azoles/macrolides inhibit; rifampin induces via PXR; grapefruit furanocoumarins irreversibly inactivate intestinal CYP3A4, altering oral first pass. CYP3A5 expression varies with genotype.

**CYP2D6.** Polymorphic with poor, intermediate, normal and ultrarapid metabolizers; largely not inducible in the usual clinical sense. It prefers many basic lipophilic amines. It O-demethylates codeine and helps produce endoxifen from tamoxifen metabolites. Fluoxetine/paroxetine can phenoconvert a normal metabolizer into a functional poor metabolizer.

**CYP2C9.** Processes S-warfarin, phenytoin and some NSAIDs. CYP2C9*2/*3 reduce activity; VKORC1 genotype also affects warfarin response by changing target sensitivity.

**CYP2C19.** Converts clopidogrel to an active thiol through two oxidation steps with contributions from other CYPs; *2 is loss-of-function, *17 increases expression. It metabolizes proton-pump inhibitors.

**CYP1A2.** Handles caffeine, theophylline and clozapine. Tobacco smoke polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons activate AhR and induce CYP1A2; nicotine itself is not the inducer. Fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin inhibit 1A2.

**Interpretation.** A substrate can be processed by multiple CYPs. Fraction metabolized (fm) matters: inhibition of a minor pathway may barely change exposure, while inhibiting a dominant pathway can matter greatly. Inhibition and induction can oppose each other over time.
levels.phd:
**Genotype is not phenotype.** CYP2D6 activity scores combine allele function and copy number; poor, intermediate, normal and ultrarapid categories predict a distribution, not a fixed clearance. Strong inhibitors cause **phenoconversion**: a genotypic normal metabolizer behaves like a poor metabolizer while inhibited. CYP2D6 is generally resistant to clinically relevant induction because its regulation differs from PXR-driven CYP3A4.

**CYP3A complexity.** CYP3A4 accommodates multiple ligands, yielding cooperative or substrate-dependent inhibition; CYP3A5's expressed *1 allele is population-variable. Gut and liver contributions must be separated. Oral midazolam probes both, IV midazolam primarily hepatic/systemic clearance; grapefruit furanocoumarins mainly affect gut 3A4 with usual intake. Induction by rifampin (PXR) can increase 3A4 expression over days; inhibition by ketoconazole is immediate and reversible, while grapefruit is mechanism-based and requires enzyme resynthesis.

**2C9 vs VKORC1.** CYP2C9*2/*3 impair S-warfarin metabolism, whereas VKORC1 variants change the target's drug sensitivity, not metabolism. Both can matter to response but answer different mechanistic questions.

**2C19 and activation.** Clopidogrel needs bioactivation via an intermediate; CYP2C19 loss-of-function is associated with reduced active-metabolite formation. Other CYPs and esterases compete, so 2C19 genotype is important but not the whole phenotype. Omeprazole is both a CYP2C19 substrate and an inhibitor; interaction interpretation depends on context.

**1A2 environmental regulation.** Combustion-derived polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, not nicotine, signal through AhR; cessation of smoking can reduce 1A2 expression and raise clozapine exposure. Cigarette-free nicotine products do not mimic this enzyme-inducing smoke effect.

**Quantitation.** Static DDI models use fm and inhibitor strength; physiologically based PK models add intestinal extraction, competitive inhibition, time-dependent inhibition, induction, genetics and unbound liver concentration. A single in vitro Ki cannot predict clinical impact without exposure and fm.
levels.expert:
**Reading a CYP report.** "Metabolized by CYP3A4" is not actionable until you know the fraction of total clearance it accounts for, whether gut first-pass matters, and whether active metabolites form. In vitro reaction phenotyping should use multiple orthogonal methods (selective inhibitor, recombinant enzyme, genotype association) because an inhibitor can hit several isoforms and recombinant rates are not native abundance.

**Clinical examples.** Codeine's CYP2D6 pathway forms morphine; poor metabolizers can get reduced effect while ultrarapid metabolizers risk greater exposure to morphine. Conversely, CYP2D6 inhibition can reduce tamoxifen endoxifen formation. CYP2C9 slow function prolongs S-warfarin exposure while VKORC1 variants alter pharmacodynamic sensitivity; do not confuse the two. Clopidogrel's activation by CYP2C19 competes with CES hydrolysis.

**Source of an interaction.** If a patient stops smoking and clozapine concentrations rise, reduced 1A2 induction is a plausible mechanism; nicotine patches do not reproduce smoke's polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Grapefruit mostly alters intestinal 3A4, so drugs given IV may respond differently from orally administered ones. An inducer takes time to change enzyme abundance; a direct inhibitor acts as drug concentration rises.

**Prioritize uncertainty.** CYP3A5 expression, transporters, hepatic function, gut absorption and co-prescribed drugs can confound genotype predictions. Report a patient's genotype and predicted phenotype separately from the measured drug concentration. Avoid extrapolating a published interaction for one substrate to every substrate of the isoform.

**Research practice.** For a new molecule, measure clearance across human hepatocyte donors with known genotypes, characterize metabolites, and model effects of strong inhibitors/inducers before committing to a single-CYP clearance route. Distribution of metabolism across enzymes is often desirable to reduce interaction vulnerability.

keyPoints: 3A4 handles many drugs in liver and gut; rifampin induces, azoles inhibit
2D6 is polymorphic and activates codeine and tamoxifen pathways
2C9 clears S-warfarin; VKORC1 affects target sensitivity, not CYP clearance
2C19 helps activate clopidogrel; *2 reduces function
1A2 metabolizes caffeine/clozapine and is induced by tobacco smoke (not nicotine)
Fraction metabolized and gut vs liver location determine interaction impact

examples.tr: The same slower enzyme can mean lower activation, not higher benefit.
Oral first-pass metabolism changes more than IV clearance.
Clozapine exposure may rise after smoke exposure stops.

test.q: Which CYP is abundant in liver and intestine and handles many drugs?
test.explain: CYP3A4 has broad specificity and contributes to both hepatic and intestinal first pass.

test.q: Which isoform is strongly polymorphic and converts codeine to morphine?
test.explain: CYP2D6 carries out this activation and has common low- or high-function variants.

test.q: CYP2C9 variation changes response to warfarin through:
test.explain: 2C9 metabolizes S-warfarin; VKORC1 is the target gene.

test.q: Which CYP genotype is important for clopidogrel activation?
test.explain: CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles reduce active-metabolite formation.

test.q: What in tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2?
test.explain: Smoke PAHs signal through AhR; nicotine itself is not the inducer.

test.q: Grapefruit furanocoumarins act mainly on:
test.explain: Intestinal CYP3A4 inactivation changes oral first-pass metabolism.

test.q: Why does inhibition of a CYP sometimes have little clinical effect?
choices: The CYP handles only a small fraction of clearance
test.explain: Fraction metabolized by the affected isoform predicts sensitivity.

test.q: Which CYP metabolizes caffeine and clozapine?
test.explain: CYP1A2 processes both and is induced by tobacco smoke.

test.q: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 in part via nuclear receptor ___.
test.explain: PXR regulates transcription of CYP3A4 and other drug-handling genes.

test.q: Name the drug target gene that affects warfarin sensitivity separately from CYP2C9 clearance.
test.explain: VKORC1 encodes the vitamin K cycle target.

test.q: A strong inhibitor can make a genetic normal metabolizer behave like a poor metabolizer: ___.
test.explain: Inhibition changes observed phenotype without changing genotype.

choices: No, different ones handle different drugs
kidTest.explain: Different CYPs have different preferences.

kidTest.explain: Some grapefruit chemicals inactivate gut CYP3A4.

advancedTest.explain: Fraction metabolized determines interaction magnitude.

lessons.title: Non-CYP oxidases (FMO, MAO, AO)

levels.kid:
CYP is not the only family that changes medicines. Your body has other workers too.

**FMO** puts oxygen on some nitrogen and sulfur atoms. One FMO changes a smelly molecule from food into a less smelly form. **MAO** breaks down certain messenger chemicals in the brain. **AO** and **XO** change other small molecules using different tools from CYP's iron.

If one worker is missing or slow, a molecule may build up. If another medicine blocks a worker, the level of its other jobs may change.

This is why scientists cannot just test CYP and say they know where a medicine goes. They have to look for all the workers that might change it. Each enzyme has its own favorite kinds of molecules.
levels.hs:
Several non-CYP enzymes oxidize drugs and natural chemicals:

- **Flavin-containing monooxygenases (FMOs)** use FAD and NADPH to add oxygen to soft nucleophiles, usually nitrogen or sulfur. Liver FMO3 converts trimethylamine to trimethylamine N-oxide. FMO3 deficiency causes trimethylaminuria, often called fish-odor syndrome.
- **Monoamine oxidases (MAO-A/B)** are FAD enzymes on the outer mitochondrial membrane. They break down neurotransmitter amines such as serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. MAO inhibitors change these pathways.
- **Aldehyde oxidase (AO)** is a cytosolic enzyme with a molybdenum cofactor that oxidizes some nitrogen-rich aromatic rings and aldehydes. It can clear candidate drugs unexpectedly.
- **Xanthine oxidase (XO)** also has molybdenum. It converts hypoxanthine and xanthine toward uric acid and metabolizes some medicines. Allopurinol blocks XO.

These enzymes do not all need the same helpers: FMO needs NADPH and O2; AO and XO use molecular oxygen as electron acceptor and do not need NADPH. MAO uses O2 to reoxidize FAD.

Testing CYPs alone can miss a major clearance route, especially for nitrogen-rich molecules prone to AO oxidation.
levels.college:
**FMO.** FMOs are microsomal FAD-dependent monooxygenases. NADPH reduces FAD; O2 forms a stable C4a-hydroperoxyflavin that transfers O to a nucleophilic N, S or P atom. FMO3 is dominant in adult liver and oxidizes trimethylamine to its N-oxide; loss of FMO3 function causes trimethylaminuria. FMO oxidation of tertiary amines may compete with CYP N-dealkylation, producing different metabolites.

**MAO.** MAO-A and MAO-B are outer-mitochondrial-membrane FAD enzymes that oxidatively deaminate monoamines. MAO-A favors serotonin and norepinephrine; both handle dopamine, while MAO-B has high activity toward phenylethylamine. Aldehyde product, ammonia and H2O2 result. Brain vs peripheral tissue distribution matters to drug effects.

**AO/XO.** Aldehyde oxidase and xanthine oxidoreductase are cytosolic molybdenum-flavin-iron–sulfur enzymes. AO oxidizes electron-poor azaheterocycles at carbons adjacent to ring N and some aldehydes. Humans and common laboratory species can differ substantially in AO activity, making animal-to-human clearance predictions difficult. Famciclovir is deacetylated then oxidized by AO to active penciclovir. XO converts hypoxanthine→xanthine→uric acid and inactivates some thiopurines. Allopurinol inhibits XO; coadministration with thiopurines can dangerously raise active-thiopurine exposure.

**ADH/ALDH.** Alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidize alcohols to aldehydes and aldehydes to acids using NAD+; they can affect drug metabolism too.

**Distinguish.** CYP and FMO often require NADPH; AO/XO activity can persist in assays without added NADPH. Cell fraction and selective inhibitors aid enzyme assignment.
levels.phd:
**Catalytic contrast.** FMO's C4a-hydroperoxyflavin is pre-formed after FAD reduction by NADPH and O2 binding, then awaits nucleophilic substrate attack; CYP Compound I forms within a heme cycle after substrate engagement. This distinction can make FMO less susceptible to classical competitive substrate inhibition, though inhibitor behavior is substrate-dependent. FMO often N-oxidizes tertiary amines and S-oxidizes thioethers; CYP may produce overlapping products, so isotope labeling and enzyme-selective systems may be needed.

**MAO mechanism and specificity.** MAO-A/B catalyze oxidative deamination of primary and secondary amines through a flavin-dependent pathway; the imine hydrolyzes to an aldehyde and ammonia or an amine. MAO-A and B have overlapping yet distinct substrate preferences. The irreversible inhibitor class can produce prolonged changes despite a short plasma half-life because enzyme synthesis is required to restore activity. Intracellular localization at the outer mitochondrial membrane affects access to substrates.

**AO unpredictability.** AOX1 oxidizes many azaheterocycles by a nucleophilic attack from molybdenum-bound hydroxide at electron-deficient carbons, followed by electron transfer through Fe-S clusters to FAD and ultimately O2. This is mechanistically unlike CYP electrophilic oxidation. AO has high human liver activity but major species differences (dogs have very low AO activity); a compound stable in canine studies can clear rapidly in humans. Zaleplon has an AO-mediated route to 5-oxo-zaleplon; famciclovir uses AO for activation after deacetylation.

**XOR.** Xanthine oxidoreductase interconverts dehydrogenase and oxidase forms; the latter uses O2 and produces ROS. XO inhibitors alter thiopurine catabolism, a serious interaction. Allopurinol itself is converted by XO to oxypurinol, another long-lasting inhibitor.

**Assay strategy.** Compare S9 and hepatocytes with microsomes. Microsomal CYP/FMO activity may be present, while cytosolic AO can be missed. NADPH dependence, selective chemical inhibitors and recombinant enzymes narrow the assignment; none alone proves it.
levels.expert:
**A development failure mode.** A nitrogen-rich heteroaromatic lead shows excellent microsomal stability but disappears rapidly in human hepatocytes. Rather than declaring the assay inconsistent, test cytosolic aldehyde oxidase. Microsomes lack most cytosolic AO activity. AO rates and metabolite patterns vary dramatically across species, so standard animal PK may not rescue a bad human prediction.

**FMO vs CYP.** A thioether produces sulfoxide under both enzyme systems; assign contributions with recombinant enzymes, appropriate inhibitors, thermal sensitivity tests and human hepatocytes. FMO3 status may vary genetically, but a single genotype does not predict all substrate kinetics. For N-oxidation, check if the N-oxide reverses or is excreted.

**MAO and brain drugs.** MAO-A/B clearance of amine neurotransmitters and drugs matters for CNS targets. Selective MAO-B inhibition can be useful therapeutically; selectivity can change with exposure and other drug combinations. Avoid assuming peripheral substrate disappearance in a liver assay reflects brain MAO.

**XO interactions.** Allopurinol or febuxostat can inhibit thiopurine inactivation; concurrent thiopurine regimens require specialist oversight. No dose estimate follows from a course note. The key mechanistic point is that blocking a clearance enzyme may sharply raise active metabolite exposure.

**AO liability response.** If an azaheterocycle has a vulnerable carbon alpha to a ring N, a substituent at that carbon or a changed ring electronics can reduce AO oxidation, but may change CYP metabolism or binding. Compare human hepatocyte intrinsic clearance and AO metabolite ID across matched pairs. Check intestinal/liver transport and free fraction before attributing everything to one enzyme.

**Big picture.** Select assays covering compartments and cofactors appropriate to the chemistry. CYP-centric screens are efficient triage, not a complete map of human metabolism.

keyPoints: FMO3 N-oxidizes trimethylamine; deficiency causes trimethylaminuria
MAO-A/B oxidatively deaminate monoamines on outer mitochondrial membranes
AOX1 oxidizes electron-poor azaheterocycles in the cytosol
AO shows major species differences and may be missed by microsomal screens
XO metabolizes purines and thiopurines; inhibitors can cause dangerous interactions
ADH/ALDH oxidize alcohols/aldehydes using NAD+

examples.tr: Deacetylation followed by AO oxidation activates this prodrug.
Both inhibit XO; XO inhibition alters thiopurine clearance.

test.q: Which enzyme converts trimethylamine to its N-oxide in adult liver?
test.explain: FMO3 uses a hydroperoxyflavin to N-oxidize trimethylamine.

test.q: MAO-A and MAO-B reside mainly on the:
test.explain: Both MAO isoforms are bound to the outer mitochondrial membrane.

test.q: What cofactor distinguishes AO chemistry from heme CYP chemistry?
test.explain: Aldehyde oxidase uses a molybdenum center along with FAD and Fe-S groups.

test.q: AO often oxidizes:
test.explain: Azaheterocycles with an electron-poor carbon near ring N are frequent substrates.

test.q: Why can microsomal stability miss an AO liability?
test.explain: Microsomes represent ER membranes, whereas AO is largely in the cytosol.

test.q: XO inhibition with a thiopurine may:
test.explain: XO normally inactivates part of thiopurine substrate; blocking it alters exposure.

test.q: Loss of FMO3 function can cause:
test.explain: Trimethylamine is no longer efficiently converted to its odorless oxide.

test.q: What three-letter abbreviation names aldehyde oxidase?
test.explain: AO is a cytosolic molybdenum-containing oxidase.

test.q: MAO oxidatively ___ monoamines.
test.explain: MAO removes amino groups via oxidation.

test.q: Which enzyme converts hypoxanthine toward uric acid?
test.explain: Xanthine oxidase participates in purine catabolism.

test.q: FMO enzymes use the flavin cofactor ___.
test.explain: Reduced FAD forms the oxygen-transfer hydroperoxyflavin.

kidTest.q: Is CYP the only body worker that changes medicines?
kidTest.explain: FMO, MAO, AO and XO are other workers.

kidTest.q: Which one works on brain messenger chemicals?
kidTest.explain: MAO breaks down certain neurotransmitter amines.

kidTest.q: FMO changes a smelly food molecule into:
kidTest.explain: FMO3 makes trimethylamine N-oxide.

kidTest.q: Are different workers good at different jobs?
kidTest.explain: Each enzyme favors different substrates.

kidTest.q: The worker abbreviated FMO is not a ___.
kidTest.explain: FMO and CYP are different enzyme families.

advancedTest.q: A lead is stable in microsomes yet clears rapidly in human hepatocytes, with an oxidized azaheterocycle product. Suspect:
advancedTest.explain: AO is cytosolic and can be absent from microsomal assays.

advancedTest.q: Why might dog PK poorly predict human AO clearance?
choices: Dogs have very low AO activity compared with humans
advancedTest.explain: Large species differences impair extrapolation.

advancedTest.q: FMO and CYP can both form sulfoxides. What distinguishes them mechanistically?
choices: FMO uses hydroperoxyflavin; CYP uses heme Compound I
advancedTest.explain: Their reactive oxygen species arise from different cofactors and cycles.

advancedTest.q: The AO enzyme that often clears human azaheterocycles is encoded by ___.
advancedTest.explain: AOX1 is human aldehyde oxidase 1.
